title: A novel series-parallel hybrid method employing fusion of deep features for air quality index forecasting
abstract: This research introduces a novel series-parallel hybrid technique for air quality index (AQI) forecasting by combining an ARFIMA model with a parallel ensemble of LSTM, ConvLSTM, BiLSTM, and CNN architectures. A novel feature fusion method is suggested to improve time series forecasting. The hybrid model can capture linear and nonlinear patterns with statistical modeling and deep feature transformation, employing dimensionality reduction and additive/multiplicative hybrid strategies. The model generates both point and interval forecasts, with forecast error distributions modeled using t location scale and gaussian distributions to construct the prediction intervals. The method is assessed using four-point and four-interval accuracy measures against three hybrid baselines, five deep learning (DL) models, and thirteen machine learning (ML) models. Tests conducted using Delhi AQI data using different train-validation-test splits show that the suggested model performs noticeably better than other ML models at multiple significance levels, exhibiting greater prediction accuracy and resilience.

title: Deep learning meets GPR: Exploring transformer models for precision soil depth prediction
abstract: Accurate soil depth mapping is vital for hydrological and ecological insights, yet traditional methods remain laborious. We integrated ground-penetrating radar (GPR) with a Transformer-based deep learning model to enhance predictions in a steep forested catchment. Using datasets comprising point-scale soil measurements and GPR transects (128 auger, 550 GPR, 678 combined points), we benchmarked the Transformer against neural networks (ANN, DNN) and machine learning models (random forest, support vector machine) under two variable strategies: all variables and Boruta-based selection. The Transformer outperformed all models across datasets and strategies, even with limited auger data. GPR data combined with all variables yielded superior predictions over Boruta-selected variables, indicating features deemed less critical in traditional models retain predictive value in Transformers. Notably, GPR integration revealed significant soil depth reductions at footslopes—undetectable with auger data alone. These findings demonstrate the enhanced accuracy of coupling GPR with Transformer models for soil depth mapping in complex terrains.

title: RECLAIM: A globally scalable machine learning framework to predict reservoir sedimentation and capacity loss from satellite-based earth observations
abstract: Most reservoirs remain poorly sampled of their actual capacity due to the high costs and logistical demands of conventional sedimentation surveys. Here, we present RECLAIM (Reservoir Estimation of Capacity Loss using AI-based Methods), a globally scalable framework to predict absolute sedimentation rates using observed records and multi-decadal Earth observations from satellite data (1984-2023). Using a dataset of 1315 observations with 88 static and dynamic catchment, climatic, and reservoir-specific features, RECLAIM integrates gradient boosting models in a dynamic ensemble, achieving a prediction RMSE of 4.44 Million Cubic Meter (MCM)/year, MAE of 1.65 MCM/year, and R2 = 0.86 on the fixed test set. Cross-validation across 10 data partitions yields RMSE = 7.62 ± 4.86 MCM/year and MAE = 3.13 ± 1.66 MCM/year, confirming stable generalization across diverse sedimentation regimes. The development of RECLAIM revealed that absolute sedimentation rate is a more robust predictand than the widely used capacity loss rate, which loses sedimentation physics when normalized by reservoir capacity. The use of RECLAIM is expected to support the long-term sustainability of reservoir infrastructure globally.

title: Physically consistent dynamic graph learning for multi-horizon nutrient prediction in a gate-controlled river network
abstract: Regulated river networks exhibit strongly nonstationary nutrient dynamics driven by time-varying hydrologic connectivity and gate operations, which challenges stable multi-horizon forecasting of Total Nitrogen (TN) and Total Phosphorus (TP). We develop the Dynamic Edge Weight and Virtual-node Spatio-Temporal Multi-Variable Gate-control Graph Neural Network (DEWV-STMV-G), a control-aware spatiotemporal graph learning framework for nutrient prediction in gate-regulated river networks. The model integrates node-wise sequential encoding for short-term hydrology–water-quality memory, basin-scale meteorology–calendar encoding for exogenous forcing and periodicity, and explicit gate-control conditioning to represent operation-dependent regime shifts. The river system is represented as a transport-consistent dynamic directed weighted graph, where edge directions follow instantaneous flow signs and edge weights vary with transport intensity and distance decay. To preserve topological closure under sparse monitoring, unobserved confluences are completed through virtual-node estimation before graph propagation. DEWV-STMV-G directly predicts TN and TP at 3, 6, 12, and 24 h horizons without recursive rollout. Using hourly observations from August 1, 2023 to September 22, 2025 and a time-ordered 80/20 train–test split, DEWV-STMV-G achieved robust multi-horizon prediction performance. On the test set, TN R2 decreased from 0.9665 at 3 h to 0.9035 at 24 h, while TP R2 decreased from 0.9665 to 0.8328, with MAE and RMSE increasing as lead time grew. The model outperformed representative spatiotemporal graph baselines and ablated variants, demonstrating the value of jointly modeling dynamic connectivity, virtual-node completion, exogenous drivers, and regulation-aware conditioning. Stratified evaluation showed that gate-opening periods were the main source of long-horizon uncertainty, whereas steady periods retained high predictive skill at 24 h. External validation in an independent regulated river network further showed averaged R2 values of 0.8250 for TN and 0.8725 for TP, providing preliminary evidence of cross-basin transferability. These results suggest that DEWV-STMV-G can support short-term forecasting and early-warning applications in regulated river-network water-quality management.

title: Improving precipitation forecasts through machine learning of the decomposed high- and low-frequency components
abstract: Traditional forecasting models decompose time series into multiple subseries but typically simulate all components using a single modeling approach. In this study, we proposed a novel methodology to disaggregate precipitation time series into distinct high- and low-frequency components and simulate them separately for different climates. We tested the proposed method on monthly and annual precipitation, representing arid, semi-arid, and humid climates in Iran. The proposed approach demonstrated superior performance compared to single model approaches. Implementing separate modeling of the components improved forecast accuracy by 39–44%. A climate-specific analysis revealed distinct performance patterns. Arid climate stations achieved high precision scores (precision = 0.83), while semi-arid stations showed a moderate accuracy (precision = 0.495). Humid climate stations maintained robust performance (precision = 0.74). The proposed two-step temporal decomposition approach can effectively address the non-stationary and random characteristics of precipitation time series, thereby improving forecast accuracy.

title: A self-supervised deep learning method for retrieving historically similar extreme rainfall patterns
abstract: Deciphering current extreme rainfall patterns through the retrieval of historical counterparts supports contextual rainfall assessment and hydrometeorological modelling. However, existing methods still struggle to capture the pronounced temporal variability and irregular spatial organization of extreme rainfall patterns, and their limited scalability hinders adaptation to growing rainfall archives. This study proposes a novel method for rainfall analog retrieval at hourly, daily, and event scales, integrating a vision transformer with masked pretraining to learn rainfall representations, an intensity-guided loss to embed hydrologic priors and emphasize extremes, and a spatiotemporal evaluation system for rainfall event evolution. Experiments demonstrate accurate and efficient retrieval of diverse rainfall patterns, with a mean query time of 21.35 ms over more than 10000 rainfall maps. The label-free method scales to expanding rainfall archives and retrieves dynamic analogues for localized extremes and rare large-scale events, extending retrieval from static pattern matching to dynamic event tracking.

title: Bias-corrected exceedance mapping of groundwater nitrate using geostatistical and machine-learning models
abstract: Spatial models used in environmental assessment are often used to predict concentrations, even when the underlying decision problem concerns the delineation of threshold exceedance areas. We show that the common practice of thresholding point predictions can introduce substantial bias in estimated exceedance areas. We propose a decision-aligned modeling and evaluation workflow that frames exceedance mapping as a probabilistic prediction task. The approach calibrates exceedance maps to match an unbiased area estimate and assesses model performance using target-weighted cross-validation. In a groundwater-nitrate case study, several widely used interpolation and machine-learning models underestimate exceedance area by 80%–98% when exceedance areas are derived by thresholding concentration predictions, despite competitive concentration-based error metrics. Area calibration removes this bias and yields a balanced trade-off between omission and commission. The workflow is model-agnostic and compatible with standard geostatistical and machine-learning methods, providing a general framework for task-aligned modeling and uncertainty quantification in environmental applications involving threshold-based decisions.

title: Coupling process-based models with machine learning for the prediction of soil carbon and nitrogen cycling
abstract: Accurate prediction of soil carbon (C) and nitrogen (N) cycling is essential for understanding ecosystem functioning, supporting sustainable agriculture, and mitigating climate change. This review summarizes recent progress in predicting soil C–N dynamics, contrasting the mechanistic fidelity yet parametric rigidity of process-based models against the predictive accuracy but limited extrapolative capacity of machine learning (ML). We synthesize specific coupling strategies, from ML-driven parameter optimization and surrogate emulation to physics-informed neural networks, highlighting their potential to improve predictive skill, scalability, and interpretability. Persistent challenges include spatial scale mismatches, increasing computational demands, and the critical need to disentangle multi-dimensional uncertainties (e.g., input, structural, and prediction errors) for large-scale applications. Finally, we outline emerging pathways, particularly the integration of multi-scale remote and proximal sensing and edge-AI frameworks, advocating an interdisciplinary research ecosystem to enable more accurate and actionable predictions of soil C–N dynamics, informing sustainable land management and food security worldwide.

title: A comparative study of deep learning and process-based models for hourly flood simulation under a unified input and optimization framework
abstract: Hourly flood forecasting is critical for disaster mitigation, yet methodological inconsistencies in input architectures and optimization algorithms often undermine comparisons between Process-Based Models (PBMs) and Deep Learning Models (DLMs). This study presents a systematic evaluation framework that standardizes these elements to ensure an equitable comparison of PBM and DLM in hourly flood simulation. We established a comparative framework incorporating four representative models: the Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) and Temporal Convolutional Network (TCN) for DLMs, alongside the HBV and Tank models for PBMs. Applied across seven Chinese catchments, our investigation yielded principal findings: (1) The GRU model, when fed with the complete flood process as input, achieved superior simulation accuracy compared to using sliding-window samples; (2) Adam is an effective method for parameter calibration within PBMs; (3) Under unified input and optimization conditions, DLMs generally achieved superior simulation performance to PBMs across most catchments.

title: What structured tool interfaces do and do not provide for LLM-based SWAT+ calibration
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly coupled with scientific simulators, yet how structured tool interfaces affect operational reliability and decision provenance remains unclear. This study introduces Hydro-MCP, a Model Context Protocol framework that constrains LLM-mediated SWAT + operation through typed function schemas, parameter-range validation, structured diagnostic feedback, and trajectory logging. We evaluated Hydro-MCP using a six-level ablation in the urban Jungnangcheon watershed, reference baselines, a rural Jiseokcheon stress test, and a held-out corruption task. In the permissive Jungnangcheon benchmark, the full Hydro-MCP configuration followed a shorter evaluation path within the tested workflow, 21.9 ± 5.3 versus 62.0 ± 16.5 model evaluations relative to unstructured LLM operation (p < 0.001), while terminal performance remained nearly unchanged (monthly NSE ≈ 0.893). A random-search baseline required fewer evaluations but achieved slightly lower terminal NSE, indicating that Hydro-MCP improves LLM-guided operation rather than non-LLM sampling efficiency. In Jiseokcheon, the full configuration achieved operational completion in all runs and Level 1 in 7 of 10 runs, whereas Levels 2-3 initiated no SWAT + simulation. This completion result concerns access to and execution of the workflow; the subsequent KGE, terminal parameters, and process-consistency analysis separately exposed zombie calibration despite acceptable fit. The corruption task further showed that logs and range constraints alone cannot detect physically corrupted model states. Within the tested workflow, the full Hydro-MCP configuration therefore improved operational control and produced reviewable provenance, while hydrological validity still required process-level consistency checks.

title: GreenHub: Toward an open platform for machine learning-based crop yield modeling and deployment
abstract: Agricultural researchers face challenges in publishing and sharing data-driven crop yield models, limiting transparency and collaboration. Additionally, collecting and preprocessing data from diverse sources is often inefficient. We present GreenHub, a first step toward a platform that streamlines both data access and model deployment for crop yield forecasting. GreenHub provides (i) public access to standardized, high-quality datasets; (ii) a uniform interface and Python-based library for flexible data retrieval; and (iii) hosting of machine learning models. Data sources include weather forecasts, soil properties, and vegetation indices. Researchers can upload models with minimal integration effort, and the platform automatically executes and visualizes model predictions for public access. This enables model comparison and fosters collaboration while saving researcher’s time. By lowering technical barriers, GreenHub offers an efficient ecosystem that lays the groundwork for developing, deploying, and sharing crop yield prediction models.

title: Individual tree mortality segmentation using a multi-task deep learning network and high-resolution aerial imagery
abstract: Accurate mapping of individual tree mortality is critical for assessing forest carbon loss, yet dead trees in aerial imagery often appear scattered, irregular, and blurred, causing high omission rates and low precision for conventional semantic segmentation models. To solve this, we propose TreeMortSeg, a tree mortality segmentation network based on multi-task learning. Structure-aware and edge-aware auxiliary learning tasks are introduced to enhance the spatial structure representation and boundary localization of dead trees. These tasks provide effective spatial geometry and contour priors for the primary segmentation task, thereby reducing omission errors and improving segmentation precision. On the TreeFinder dataset, TreeMortSeg achieved the best dead tree F1-score (66.29%) and IoU (49.57%), outperforming the second-best model (DeepLabV3+) by 6.9 and 7.3 percentage points, respectively. Furthermore, it demonstrated strong robustness across diverse forest conditions and superior cross-regional generalizability. This research supports precise large-scale tree mortality mapping and reliable forest carbon loss assessment.

title: PM2.5 concentration prediction method based on laplacian-enhanced multi-pooling spatio-temporal self-attention
abstract: Rapid urbanization exacerbates air pollution and endangers public health and economy. Accurate short-term PM2.5 prediction supports pollution control, policy-making and regional environmental governance. Driven by emissions, regional transport and meteorology, PM2.5 exhibits complex nonlinear spatiotemporal patterns. Existing models suffer defects in graph construction, spatiotemporal fusion and long-term temporal modeling. This work presents LGMPST, a spatiotemporal graph network integrating Laplacian probabilistic attention, graph-convolutional up-down mapping and multi-perspective pooling. Tested on 36 Beijing monitoring stations, LGMPST surpasses LSTM, AirFormer, STiTransformer and other advanced baselines. Seasonal comparison, multi-station tests, pollution-stratified evaluation and ablation studies validate its performance. Cross-regional experiments over Beijing-Tianjin-Hebei and Guangzhou further confirm generalizability for refined air-quality forecasting and joint governance.

title: Knowledge-guided graph time-series modelling for regional carbon emission prediction and decision support: An integrated assessment of carbon peaking pathways in Guangxi
abstract: Accurate long-horizon carbon-emission forecasting requires models that capture inter-city dependence, remain robust under recursive prediction, and separate model outputs from policy targets. This study develops a Knowledge-Guided Graph Time-Series (KG-GraphTS) framework for 14 prefecture-level cities in Guangxi, China, using a 2000–2024 panel of socioeconomic, energy, industrial, demographic, remote-sensing, and climate variables. Secondary-industry GDP is incorporated both as a predictor and as structural knowledge for an economic-knowledge graph combining economic gravity, industrial-structure similarity, and geographical proximity. The model integrates graph convolution, a two-layer GRU, city-specific autoregressive residual learning, City-Specific Bias, and soft knowledge-guided regularization. A leakage-controlled chronological design is used for training, recursive validation, and held-out testing, while future emissions are projected under Baseline, Low-Carbon, High-Carbon, and Carbon-Neutrality-oriented scenarios without imposing terminal policy targets. KG-GraphTS achieves R2 = 0.9900 and RMSE = 2.1846 Mt under rolling evaluation and retains R2 = 0.9679 and RMSE = 3.9085 Mt under fixed-origin recursive testing. Under the Carbon-Neutrality-oriented scenario, emissions peak at 455.77 Mt in 2034 and decline to 165.90 Mt by 2060, a 63.6% reduction, yet all cities peak after 2030. Under the Baseline scenario, all cities reach Alert by 2030 and cumulative emissions exceed the Carbon-Neutral reference budget by 15.46 Gt CO2. These results support robust target-independent forecasting and transparent scenario-based decision support with explicit uncertainty and pathway diagnostics.

title: PatchX: A dual-branch embedding framework with cross-attention for streamflow forecasting
abstract: Accurate streamflow forecasting is critical for flood management, yet hydrological models based on deep learning face an architectural dilemma: channel-mixing models may obscure heterogeneous hydrological signals through shared representations, while channel-independent architectures fail to explicitly capture causal rainfall-runoff mechanisms. We propose PatchX, a hydrologically structured dual-branch framework that separately encodes antecedent streamflow and meteorological information. This separation preserves runoff continuity while reducing interference from heterogeneous inputs. Multi-scale meteorological embeddings represent different response lags, and asymmetric cross-attention uses the runoff-state representation to select and incorporate relevant meteorological variables and temporal scales. Evaluated across six diverse basins (1- to 7-day lead times), PatchX consistently outperformed baselines, surpassing iTransformer and PatchTST by up to 7.82% and 3.78% in KGE. Furthermore, SHAP-based interpretability and ablation studies revealed that PatchX mitigates "attention collapse" and constructs internal mathematical representations that more closely align with physical and hydrological principles, providing a robust paradigm for streamflow forecasting.
